items.title: How much traffic does a bad deploy actually reach at each canary size?
items.description: Grounded in this unit's Scenario: the checkout regression that hit 400 real customers when the canary was 5% of a 8,000-request traffic window. Drag the canary's starting traffic percentage to see how many customers a bad deploy reaches before the SLO alert can catch it — this is the direct, concrete cost of skipping a small first stage, the exact gap between Team A's 100% exposure and Team B's 5% one.
items.compute: const totalRequestsInWindow = 8000; const customersExposed = Math.round(totalRequestsInWindow * (params.canaryTrafficPercent / 100)); return { customersExposed };

outputs.label: Customers exposed to the bug before detection

items.title: How does incident duration shrink as each integrated safety layer gets added?
items.description: Grounded in this unit's Team A vs. Team B comparison: Team A (0 layers) took about 72 minutes to reach safety; Team B (all 4 layers — config validation, canary, SLO alerting, compatible rollback) took about 10 minutes. Drag the number of layers actually wired in to see the expected time-to-safe for the same underlying bug — this reproduces L1's two endpoints as one continuous relationship instead of just two isolated data points.

params.name: layersEnabled
params.label: Integrated safety layers enabled (of 4: config validation, canary, SLO alerting, compatible rollback)

items.compute: const noLayersMinutes = 72; const allLayersMinutes = 10; const minutesToSafe = Math.round(noLayersMinutes - (noLayersMinutes - allLayersMinutes) * (params.layersEnabled / 4)); return { minutesToSafe };
